topics: 🔥 Piggul Intent on Lost or Burned Portions — 'about to be lost' vs. actually gone, reconciled with Rabbi Yoḥanan's limit
🩸 Rav Pappa's Distinction — sprinkling helps meat that left the courtyard only if the blood itself never left
👥 Rabbi Elazar's Qualification — Rabbi Akiva's kal vaḥomer only works when two sin offerings were slaughtered simultaneously
📖 The Story of Kfar Pani — an old man's challenge, the Galilee colleagues' doubt, and Reish Lakish's charge of a 'stolen answer'
⚖️ New Mishna: Leniency AND Stringency vs. All Stringency — how sprinkling's effect differs for offerings of the most sacred order and offerings of lesser sanctity

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Pressure-Testing Rabbi Akiva's Rule on Sprinkling
overview.subtitle: Meilah 7a–7b
overview.hebrewSource: יֵשׁ מַעֲשֵׂה דָמִים בְּקׇדְשֵׁי קָדָשִׁים לְהָקֵל וּלְהַחֲמִיר, וּבְקָדָשִׁים קַלִּים כּוּלְּהוּ לְהַחֲמִיר
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf continues probing the limits of Rabbi Akiva's position that sprinkling can still work even for meat that already left the Temple courtyard. Rav Pappa narrows it further: sprinkling only helps if the blood itself stayed inside while the meat left — not if the blood itself left. Rabbi Elazar likewise limits Rabbi Akiva's kal vaḥomer proof to sin offerings slaughtered at the same moment. A memorable story has Rabbi Shimon carrying a skeptical question from an old man in Kfar Pani, through doubting colleagues in the Galilee, to Rabbi Akiva himself — whose answer Reish Lakish later calls 'a stolen response,' prompting Rabbi Yoḥanan to defend it. The daf closes with a new mishna mapping out, in detail, exactly when sprinkling helps (leniency) and when it hurts (stringency) for both categories of offerings.

slides.title: 🔥 Can Piggul Intent Apply to Portions Already Lost or Burned?
slides.subtitle: Reconciling a baraita with Rabbi Yoḥanan's limit on Rabbi Akiva's rule

steps.content: 1️⃣ Baraita: one can render an offering piggul by intent, 'even regarding portions already lost or burned'

2️⃣ Challenge: if lost/burned portions (not 'in the world') can still be affected by intent, doesn't that mean sprinkling works even when the WHOLE offering is gone — against Rabbi Yoḥanan's limit to 'partly left'?
3️⃣ Supporting evidence: Rabbi Zeira reminds Rav Asi that blood destined to be poured out (נשפכין) has 'no substance' — so intent shouldn't apply to it either, just as with anything truly gone
4️⃣ Rava's fix: emend the baraita to read 'portions about to be lost or burned' — not yet destroyed, so intent still applies; once truly gone, intent does not

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: The apparent contradiction dissolves — Rabbi Yoḥanan's limit (Rabbi Akiva's rule works only when part of the offering remains) stands intact.

slides.title: 🩸 Rav Pappa: It's the Blood That Must Stay
slides.subtitle: A further narrowing of Rabbi Akiva's rule
slides.hebrewSource: שָׁחַט בִּשְׁתִיקָה וְיָצָא דָּם, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחָזַר וּזְרָקוֹ – לֹא עָשָׂה וְלֹא כְלוּם
slides.label: The rule:
slides.text: Rav Pappa teaches that Rabbi Akiva's ruling — that sprinkling can still exempt meat which left the courtyard — applies only when the meat left while the blood remained inside and was properly sprinkled. But if the blood itself left the courtyard, even bringing it back in and sprinkling it accomplishes nothing: a supporting baraita confirms that sacred-order meat stays subject to me'ilah, and lesser-sanctity portions stay exempt from me'ilah, exactly as if no sprinkling had occurred at all.

slides.title: 👥 Rabbi Akiva's Kal VaḤomer — With or Without Rabbi Elazar's Limit
slides.subtitle: Does the timing of slaughter matter?

lines.speaker: R' Akiva
lines.text: Two sin offerings stand fit — one originally lost, one designated in its place. Sprinkling one animal's blood exempts even the OTHER animal's meat from me'ilah. So it certainly should exempt its own meat, even if that meat left the courtyard.

lines.speaker: R' Elazar
lines.text: That kal vaḥomer only works when both animals were slaughtered at the same time — treated then as a single body. If slaughtered one after the other, Rabbi Akiva agrees the rule does not apply.

lines.speaker: Reish Lakish (citing R' Oshaya)
lines.text: Rabbi Akiva actually gave his student Rabbi Shimon a 'stolen' (misleading) answer! If the second animal is unfit either way, why should simultaneous vs. sequential slaughter matter at all?

lines.speaker: R' Yoḥanan
lines.text: But you yourself distinguish the same way elsewhere! Consider two guarantee guilt offerings, slaughtered together, where one's portions ascend the altar before the other's blood is sprinkled — you'd agree those portions must descend, proving sequential rites are NOT treated as one body.

callout.label: Outcome:
callout.text: Reish Lakish is silenced by Rabbi Yoḥanan's proof — 'we have cut off the legs of the child,' as Rabbi Yoḥanan puts it.

slides.title: 📖 The Story of Kfar Pani
slides.subtitle: A question travels from a village elder, through skeptical colleagues, to Rabbi Akiva

nodes.content: 👴 An old man in Kfar Pani asks Rabbi Shimon: did Rabbi Akiva really say sprinkling helps meat that already left the courtyard?
🗣️ Rabbi Shimon confirms: yes. His Galilee colleagues object: 'It's unfit — how can sprinkling accept the unfit?'
🎓 Rabbi Shimon brings the challenge directly to Rabbi Akiva himself
💡 Rabbi Akiva: 'Don't you already accept that one animal's sprinkling exempts an unfit SECOND animal's meat (the lost/found sin offering case)? By kal vaḥomer, it should exempt its own meat too.'

callout.label: Later critique:
callout.text: This is the very exchange Reish Lakish calls a 'stolen answer' — because it doesn't explain why simultaneous vs. sequential slaughter should matter, a gap Rabbi Yoḥanan closes in the debate above.

slides.title: ⚖️ New Mishna: Where Sprinkling Helps and Where It Hurts
slides.subtitle: Kodshei kodashim has both leniency and stringency; kodashim kalim has only stringency
rows: Still subject to me'ilah (never permitted to anyone)
NOT subject to me'ilah (now permitted to priests) — the 'leniency'
NOT subject to me'ilah (never consecrated until sprinkled)
Portions become subject to me'ilah; meat does not — the 'stringency'
Full piggul, notar, and tamei liability applies once sprinkling occurs

callout.label: Gemara's coda:
callout.text: Rabbi Ḥanina explains the mishna's 'not subject to me'ilah' for lesser-sanctity meat after sprinkling still carries a real prohibition when that meat had left the eating area before sprinkling — following Rabbi Akiva's view that sprinkling's effect on meat that left concerns only when it may finally be burned, not that it is fully permitted.

summary.principle: Rabbi Akiva's rule that sprinkling can rescue meat which already left the Temple courtyard is repeatedly narrowed — it requires the blood itself to have stayed inside, and (per Rabbi Elazar) requires simultaneous slaughter in the two-offerings proof — while the new mishna maps a clean asymmetry: sprinkling is a leniency for sacred-order meat but a pure stringency for lesser-sanctity portions.

flowSteps.content: 🔥 Piggul intent applies to portions 'about to be' lost/burned, not to portions already gone
🩸 Rav Pappa: sprinkling only rescues meat that left if the BLOOD stayed inside the courtyard

columns.content: 👥 R' Elazar: R' Akiva's kal vaḥomer needs simultaneous slaughter of both sin offerings
📖 Kfar Pani story: R' Akiva's answer defended by R' Yoḥanan against Reish Lakish's critique

flowSteps.content: ⚖️ New Mishna: sacred-order meat gets a leniency after sprinkling; lesser-sanctity offerings get only a stringency
🎓 Key Principle: sprinkling's power to rescue meat from me'ilah is real but narrowly bounded — the blood must never have left, and the offerings must share one moment of slaughter

quiz.q: How does Rava resolve the apparent contradiction between a baraita (piggul intent applies to 'lost or burned' portions) and Rabbi Yoḥanan's rule that sprinkling only helps when part of an offering remains?
o: He says the baraita is entirely false
He emends the baraita to mean portions that are 'about to be' lost or burned, not yet actually destroyed
He says piggul never applies to lost portions
He says Rabbi Yoḥanan's rule is incorrect
quiz.e: Rava reinterprets the baraita's wording so it refers to portions still present but destined for loss or burning — resolving the contradiction while preserving Rabbi Yoḥanan's limit.

quiz.q: According to Rav Pappa, when is Rabbi Akiva's rule that sprinkling exempts meat that left the courtyard actually effective?
o: Only if the meat left while the blood remained inside and was properly sprinkled — not if the blood itself left
In every case, regardless of where the blood was
Only for offerings of lesser sanctity
Only if the meat was returned before sunset
quiz.e: Rav Pappa teaches that sprinkling rescues meat that left only when the blood stayed inside the courtyard; if the blood itself left, sprinkling accomplishes nothing even if the blood is later brought back and sprinkled.

quiz.q: What limitation does Rabbi Elazar place on Rabbi Akiva's kal vaḥomer proof from the two sin offerings?
o: It only applies to burnt offerings
It only works if both animals were slaughtered at the same time, not one after the other
It only applies to guilt offerings
There is no limitation; it always applies
quiz.e: Rabbi Elazar restricts the proof to a case of simultaneous slaughter, treating the two animals as one body; sequential slaughter means the second is already unfit before the first's blood is even sprinkled.

quiz.q: What criticism does Reish Lakish (citing Rav Oshaya) raise against Rabbi Akiva's answer to Rabbi Shimon in the Kfar Pani story, and how does Rabbi Yoḥanan respond?
o: Reish Lakish says the story never happened; Rabbi Yoḥanan agrees

Reish Lakish calls it a 'stolen answer' since the timing of slaughter shouldn't matter if the second animal is unfit regardless; Rabbi Yoḥanan shows Reish Lakish himself relies on the same simultaneous/sequential distinction elsewhere
Reish Lakish says Rabbi Akiva contradicts himself about piggul; Rabbi Yoḥanan agrees
Reish Lakish says the old man in Kfar Pani was not a valid witness
quiz.e: Reish Lakish calls the answer deceptive because it doesn't explain why timing matters; Rabbi Yoḥanan silences him by showing that even Reish Lakish accepts a simultaneous-vs-sequential distinction in the case of two guarantee guilt offerings.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, what is unique about the sprinkling of blood for offerings of the most sacred order compared to offerings of lesser sanctity?
o: Sprinkling is only a stringency for both categories

For sacred-order offerings, sprinkling brings both leniency (removing meat from me'ilah) and stringency (piggul/notar/tamei liability); for lesser-sanctity offerings, sprinkling brings only stringency
Sprinkling has no effect on either category
Sprinkling only matters for offerings of lesser sanctity
quiz.e: The mishna states that sprinkling for sacred-order offerings is both a leniency (exempting the meat from me'ilah) and a stringency (creating piggul/notar/tamei liability), while for lesser-sanctity offerings it is entirely a stringency, since those offerings were never subject to me'ilah before sprinkling.
